title: Writing a feature page a salesperson can send
metaTitle: A feature page sales can send
excerpt: A feature page worth sending covers one feature, the job it finishes, who it is for, and a picture of it in use. A page that lists every capability is a sitemap.
alt: A bright office window ledge with a laptop, a closed notebook, white chairs, and a tall indoor tree, a single calm page someone could send to one buyer.
caption: A ledge, a laptop, and one notebook. One feature, on a page a salesperson can send. Photograph via Unsplash.

faqs.question: What belongs on a feature page a salesperson can send?
faqs.answer: One job, the person it is for, a picture of that job in the product, the boundary, and one next step. The heading should be the job, not the internal module name. A list of every capability is a sitemap, and people do not forward sitemaps.

faqs.question: How is a feature page different from a help doc?
faqs.answer: A help doc teaches someone who already has an account which control to click. A feature page explains the job to someone who was not on the sales call. Link to the help doc if the steps are long. Do not make the help doc the first explanation.

faqs.question: Who should be allowed to publish a feature page?
faqs.answer: An owner, working from one template, who checks the boundary, the picture, and the plan name. Update the picture in the same week the interface changes, or take the page down. Sales preambles pasted above the link are a review of the writing. Use them.

sources.title: Influencing your title links in search results
How Long Do Users Stay on Web Pages?

markdown:
A feature page a salesperson can send does one job. It explains one feature, the work that feature finishes, who it is for, and what to do next. It includes a picture of the feature in use. A saas feature page that lists every capability is a sitemap with nicer type. The buyer will not forward a sitemap to their boss. They will forward a page that answers the question they were just asked.

Write the page for the moment after a call, when someone who was not on the call has to understand a single thing. That constraint keeps the page short enough to be believed.

## One feature, named as a job

Pick the feature the way a buyer picks it. Not the internal module name. The job. "Assign an overdue order." "Export the month for your bookkeeper." "See which clinic has not finished notes." If the internal name is obscure, it can appear once, in a quiet line, for the champion who has to match it to your UI. The heading is the job.

Say who it is for in the first paragraph. A warehouse lead. A finance partner. A clinician. If two roles use it differently, you may need two pages, or one page with a clear primary role and a short note for the second. A page addressed to "teams" is a page addressed to no one.

Say what it does not do. One sentence. "This does not replace your accounting system. It sends the file your accountant already knows how to open." Boundaries make a salesperson brave. Without them, the sender hedges in the email and the page becomes decoration.

Google's guidance on title links applies directly. The title element should describe this feature, in concise language, and it should not share a boilerplate suffix with every other feature page. "Assign overdue orders" is a title. "Platform features, modules, solutions, and tools" is a title that makes every result from your site look the same. The visible heading and the title should agree, so Google is not left to guess which line is the real one.

Keep the URL readable. A slug with the job survives a paste into a chat. A slug full of tracking parameters looks like a trap. Put tracking in the salesperson's sending tool if you must. Leave the public URL clean.

## The picture has to be the feature

Show the screen where the job happens. Crop to the control, the list, or the confirmation. A full-product tourist shot at low contrast does not survive Slack's preview, and it does not survive a phone.

Use a believable state. The buyer's colleague should recognize the kind of data, even if the names are examples. If you must anonymize, keep the shape of the truth: long names, a zero, a date format your market uses. A perfect table of round numbers reads as a mock, and mocks get discounted.

Caption it with the outcome. "The oldest order is at the top. Assigning it clears it from this list." The caption is what a skimmer reads. Nielsen Norman Group notes that people often leave in 10 to 20 seconds and read only about a quarter of the text. The heading, the caption, and the button may be the only things that land. They have to carry the job on their own.

Do not surround the picture with badges, confetti, or a second product you wish they had asked about. The salesperson can link to another feature page. This page stays loyal to the question that prompted the send.

If the feature is a flow, two images are the maximum before you are writing a manual. Before and after. Or the setup and the daily use, if those are genuinely different. A six-step gallery belongs in the product's help, linked from here, not in the sales page itself.

## What the salesperson needs around the picture

A short opening they do not have to apologize for. Four to seven sentences. The job, who it is for, the boundary, and the next step. Write it in the voice of the site, which should be the voice of a careful person. A page that suddenly becomes a pitch deck will embarrass the sender who promised "I'll send you something plain."

The requirement, if there is one. Plan, role, or connected system. "Available on the operations plan. An admin turns it on." Hidden requirements are how a forwarded page creates a messy second call. Put them in the open.

A single next step. Book time, start a trial, or reply with the file you need. Match the step to the way you actually sell. If this feature is never bought self-serve, do not put a self-serve button that dead-ends. If it is self-serve, do not force a "request a demo" on a reader who was ready to turn it on.

A way to the rest of the product that does not hijack the page. One link: all features, or the homepage, or pricing. The salesperson's email can add context. The page should not be a second homepage.

Proof, if you have it, in one line. A type of team, a before and after you can defend, a constraint. No invented quotation. No trophy count you would not say out loud to a skeptical operator. If you have no proof yet, the screen is the proof. Do not decorate the absence.

Hanabi would build this as a template, not as a one-off art direction for every feature. Same type, same width, same place for the picture and the boundary. Next.js and a small set of components keep the pages from drifting into twelve layouts. The drift is how a library becomes unsendable. A founder should be able to preview a new feature page and know where the sentence goes.

## Pages that are not this page

The homepage shows the product as a whole and speaks to the audience that pays. It is a poor leave-behind for a single question. If your homepage is the only URL sales will send, the feature is not legible enough yet.

The help doc teaches a logged-in user to click the right control. It assumes they already bought. Sending a help doc to a prospect is sometimes right, late in the process. It is a poor first explanation, because it starts in the middle.

The changelog says what is new. A prospect does not care that you shipped it on a Thursday. They care that they can do the job. You can link to the note. Do not make the note the sales page.

The pricing page explains money. Link to it when the feature's plan is part of the decision. Do not paste three tiers under every feature. You will create contradictions the moment one tier changes. One link, with the plan name in the sentence beside it, stays true longer.

A comparison page can exist if you can be precise and fair. It is not the feature page. Buyers who want a comparison will ask. Give them a page that does that job, and keep this one on the feature.

## A page that survives being forwarded

Assume the buyer will paste the link into a thread with one sentence of their own, or with none. The page has to make sense to a person who missed the call. That means the first paragraph repeats the job, even if the salesperson already said it. Repetition here is a service. It is not padding.

Check the preview. The title, the opening line, and the image are what most chat tools will show. If the image is a wide desktop crop, the preview will be a blur. A tighter crop of the actual control is a better ambassador. Write alt text that states the job the screen shows, so the preview is not the only way the picture exists.

Keep the page fast enough that a person on a phone, between meetings, does not abandon it before the picture arrives. web.dev's loading threshold is a useful bar: largest contentful paint within 2.5 seconds for a good experience, measured for most users rather than on a studio laptop. A feature page with a cinematic background and a tiny UI has the priorities backward. The UI is the content.

Ask one colleague who does not sell the feature to read the page and say the job back to you. If they add capabilities you did not mention, the page is leaking into a sitemap. Cut until they repeat the one job. If they cannot find who it is for, the first paragraph is still too polite.

## How sales and the site stay in step

Read the page in the tools your team actually uses to send it. Slack, email, a phone. The first lines and the image preview are the product in those contexts. Rewrite the opening until it makes sense with no decoration around it.

Ask a salesperson which sentence they delete before they send the page. Delete it on the page, or fix it until they would leave it. The private preamble they paste above the link is a review of your writing. Collect those preambles for a week. They are the brief.

Decide who may publish a feature page. A template helps. A template without an owner becomes a dump of half-features and internal names. The owner checks the boundary, the picture, and the plan name. The picture gets updated when the UI changes, in the same week, or the page comes down.

Keep the words in a place the team can edit. A marketing site built so a non-developer can change a sentence will stay closer to the truth. On a Hanabi project the client owns the repo and the content, and the portal holds the notes after delivery. The feature page is one of those contents. It should not require a release to fix a verb.

Review the set as a set. Read only the headings. If two features promise the same job, merge the pages or distinguish them. Sales will not choose carefully. They will send the first result, and the buyer will notice the overlap even if your team has stopped seeing it.

When the feature is really a question about money, and you cannot print a number, the next page has a different shape. The piece on [the page that explains pricing without a number](/blog/the-page-that-explains-pricing-without-a-number) is the next read. A feature page should link there rather than inventing a price in a caption.

If you want help shaping one feature into a page someone can forward without a disclaimer, book [an intro call](https://cal.com/hanabi/30min). Bring the feature, the boundary, and the sentence sales currently paste above the link.
